articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report
articles.subtitle: china Apple Intelligence Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence

china

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Hands-On with Computer History: OpenAI’s Take on Agent Memory
articles.subtitle: Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into...
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

The user continued writing computer history. md in Obsidian’s MacStories Vault, refining the section that explains how Computer History differs from the earlier Chronicle preview and adding a practical description of what the feature records while the user works.

The user referenced the OpenAI Learn Computer History documentation in Safari, briefly exchanged messages with Federico Viticci, checked ChatGPT/Codex settings, and then opened MacStories Images to queue a screenshot named CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png for upload. The upload was queued by the end of the segment, but no completed upload or copied Markdown image link was observed.

You’ll also find details that ChatGPT deems important and non-obvious, such as the following:

Important non-obvious context about the user MacStories Vault - Obsidian vault where the Computer History article draft was active. computer history. md - active note being drafted for the Computer History article. CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png - screenshot selected from @ Screenshots and queued in MacStories Images near the end of the window.

MacStories Images - internal Safari image uploader used for the screenshot; the page showed one queued item and an Upload 1 control. Federico Viticci - Messages conversation briefly active during the writing session. ChatGPT/Codex settings - ChatGPT app showed settings around 10:08Z, likely related to the same Computer History article context.

Important non-obvious context about the user

MacStories Vault - Obsidian vault where the Computer History article draft was active.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: FFXIV’s Switch 2 Version Might Be the Best It’s Ever Been (For Casuals)
articles.subtitle: For me. It's a different story for hardcore players Nintendo had a poor reputation for online stability during the Switch 1 era.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
For me. It's a different story for hardcore players

Nintendo had a poor reputation for online stability during the Switch 1 era. Mario Kart 8 matches frequently disconnected, Mario Party online was a nightmare, and even Splatoon 3 suffered from regular issues. So I was surprised and more than a little apprehensive when Square Enix announced it was releasing the always-online MMO Final Fantasy XIV for Switch 2.

After spending two weeks with FFXIV on Switch 2, though, I'm sorely tempted to put up with the extra sub and just make this the main way I play the game. Depending on how you play FFXIV, though, you might want to stick with whatever platform you're on now.

So, the basic bits first. Connection issues were nonexistent in the two weeks I've played FFXIV on Switch 2, following its Aug. 1 release. Load times are comparable to other platforms. Traveling to and from other data centers was seamless. I progressed through a good chunk of Heavensward on one of my alt characters, and did some sightseeing in Dawntrail 's Tural and thoroughly enjoyed the freedom of playing on Nintendo's hybrid platform.

I've played FFXIV on an Asus ROG Ally before, and it's fine. But the Switch 2 is, for me, a less clunky device that's easier to hold and has fewer chances for things to go awry. It's also where I do most of my gaming now, so playing FFXIV untethered to my computer and free to swap to Cyberpunk 2077 or Mario Kart World or whatever else took my fancy without having to even change consoles was the kind of lazy I long for in my leisure time.

There are drawbacks, of course. Draw distance isn't the best on Switch 2 in handheld mode, though how much you notice this depends on where in the game world you are. It's easier to see in open areas like Thanalan and La Noscea, where trees and other far-off objects appear and disappear in ways you just don't have to deal with on other platforms.

They are far-off, though, and in less barren zones, like Dawntrail 's Kozama'uka and Yak'tel, object placement hides the horizon, and subsequently the pop-in, anyway. Up close, everything looks lovely, and the graphics improvements Square Enix made when Dawntrail launched — especially the flora and foliage improvements — are noticeable even in handheld mode.

Recommended For You

Performance is solid where it counts, though: in battle, in dungeons, and in most multi-person boss fights. Square Enix locked the frame rate at 30 frames per second. That sounds terribly low for a game in 2026 and even a bit damning when you consider FFXIV launched over 10 years ago. But it's a target the game can hit more often than not, and, for me anyway, it's easy to overlook after a short adjustment period.

Populated areas put more of a strain on things, though it depends on just how populated the location is. The hub city Limsa Lominsa in my home world on Dynamis (something of a rural backwater in terms of FFXIV population) has a middling amount of people at any given time, including a troupe of Viera performing EZ-dance routines on the walls and bedecked with fairy wings. Everything here is smooth.

I traveled to the much more heavily populated Faerie on the Aether server to test matchmaking, and Limsa there was rather a different story. So many people crammed into the plaza that I could see them vanishing as the game tried managing the visual load, and still the frame rate dipped.

But I am not part of a dancing troupe regaling the plainfolk with my smooth moves and glittery wings. I spend almost no time in city hub areas on any world, so this social scenario was, at worst, a minor annoyance. Fates ( FFXIV 's event battles in open field areas) and other, less congested social activities unfolded with no issue at all, even with chaotic weather conditions in play like the fog in Mor Dhona.

The caveat to all this praise is that I'm not a high-level raider, and the 72-player Frontline PvP matches confuse me. I do the easy raids, sometimes, and dip my toes into PvP for fast job leveling. But I mostly play for story, crafting, vibes — all the casual stuff. If the hardcore battles are more your thing, you might want to keep playing on whatever platform you're already using.

I ran the Crystal Tower Alliance Raid again to see how things went, and minus a few brief stutters when animations literally filled the screen, everything ran smoothly. The screen-filling was a bigger issue, though. 24-person raids are chaos at the best of times, but when I played it in handheld mode on the smaller screen, I couldn't see anything other than bright lights and shifting colors.

Lower difficulty and more people to carry you mean that's fine in the Crystal Tower, the game's only mandatory raid. Elsewhere? I'm not so sure this is the experience you want when you're staring down Savage Kefka.

Performance was more frequently choppy in the Frontline matches I attempted, and identifying a target or keeping track of allies was functionally impossible once the spells and combat animations started. You can, of course, turn the effects off, but where's the fun in that? I enjoy the drama and spectacle. Playing in docked mode on a decent-sized (27-inch) monitor made the visual clutter less pronounced, though.

For casuals like me, FFXIV on Switch 2 is excellent. It's stable where it needs to be and looks great, and the convenience of long docked sessions or quick handheld adventures is hugely appealing. It's definitely not the way to play for endgame challenges or dedicated socializing, but this is probably where I'll first dive into Evercold when it launches next year.

And defied one of fantasy's most restrictive tropes

articles.title: If you’re traveling in the Apple ecosystem, this is the tech you need to pack
articles.subtitle: Macworld One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives).
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives). We try to go on a big international trip every 18 months or so—I went to South Africa in 2024, and I just got back from a trip to Iceland in August to see the eclipse. And I always take a lot of gear with me.

Every great trip requires planning, whether it’s an overnight stay an hour away from home or a grand vacation in a country I’ve never visited before. Besides all the travel logistics (that my wife handles), there’s the tech you need to bring, which is my responsibility in my household.

Over the years, I’ve figured out what tech I absolutely need to take with me. There’s an art to figuring out what to bring. You don’t want to overdo it, because you’ll end up lugging around stuff you aren’t using. But you don’t want to be left without that thing you absolutely need and don’t really have a means of obtaining that item where you are.

While I now rely on my iPhone for all the photos and videos I shoot, I need other items to ensure a successful and enjoyable trip. Here’s a list of the gear I bring with me on my trips. This is the stuff I almost always bring no matter where I’m going. Hopefully, you can use this list to help you figure out what you need to bring on your next trip. Even with a recent $100 price hike, the MacBook Neo is such a delight–lightweight, fast, and durable. And as I point out in my review, it doesn’t need to be a secondary machine—the Neo is extremely capable of being a daily-use Mac.

Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

articles.title: "Through the looking glass": as Arkane fight for their future, Dishonored veteran Harvey Smith reveals new studio dedicated to immersive sims
articles.subtitle: Expect "imaginative first-person action RPGs" with "well-realised worlds" and "expressive" systems Days after Deus Ex director Warren Spector announced that he was quitting the business, another former Ion Storm developer, Harvey Smith, has revealed Black...
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Expect "imaginative first-person action RPGs" with "well-realised worlds" and "expressive" systems

Days after Deus Ex director Warren Spector announced that he was quitting the business, another former Ion Storm developer, Harvey Smith, has revealed Black Pony Immersive - a new studio dedicated to the creation of "imaginative first-person action RPGs set within well-realized worlds, where players create their own memorable experiences with expressive, emergent game systems.

" The announcement features the maxim: "through the looking glass, we’re chasing a dream of mystery, meaning, and creative play. " Hey, I understood that reference! Sure sounds like an imsim shop to me.

Black Pony are based, or at least, "centralised" out in Austin, Texas. Smith is joined in the cockpit by a couple of other former Arkane developers, Ben Horne and Ricardo Bare. The studio's wider workforce are located around the United States, and include people who've spent time at Spider-Man makers Insomniac, Fortnite wranglers Epic, Just Cause inventors Avalanche, and Saints Row... bejanglers Volition.

It's a hopeful turn of events because it wasn't long ago that Microsoft closed Arkane Austin, creators of the very good Prey 2017 and the sadly not very good Redfall. Nic (RPS in peace) had thoughts. Microsoft are currently taking the axe to what's left of Arkane in Lyon – as of writing, the developers are haggling out the terms of their sale, closure or buyout with the Xbox team. Smith alludes to this in a forgiveably buzzwordy press release.

“During a time of industry volatility, I'm proud to announce the next step in my video game journey with the reveal of our new studio,” he writes. “This effort reflects everything we've learned, and all we hold dear. My favorite gaming memories come from seeing players approach challenges with creativity, deep-diving into our world building. We try to reward players for their curiosity and exploration. At our new studio, we're building exactly the kind of single-player games we're most passionate about.”

The developers don't have a game to reveal as yet, but Horne notes that "this group has worked together for years, decades in some cases, and is purpose-built to make the ambitious games we love - immersive sims". We can expect more details "soon". Dear Mr Horne: please can I have an immersive sim that takes place entirely inside the squirming, reactive innards of a very large whale, like the horrible leviathans from Dishonored. We could call it "Jonah's Ex" or "The Xbox Acquisition Experience".

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: STALKER 2: Cost of Hope review: An expanded Zone that begs to be explored, even as its faction war fizzles
articles.subtitle: Friendlies in Chorno? Developer: GSC Game World Publisher: GSC Game World Release: August 20th 2026 On: Windows From: Steam, GOG, Epic Games Store Price: TBC Reviewed on: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Nvidia RTX 5080, 32GB RAM, Windows 11 Like the technical fix-uppery...
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Friendlies in Chorno?

Developer: GSC Game World

Publisher: GSC Game World

Release: August 20th 2026

On: Windows

From: Steam, GOG, Epic Games Store

Price: TBC

Reviewed on: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Nvidia RTX 5080, 32GB RAM, Windows 11

Like the technical fix-uppery of the 2.0 update it’s launching alongside, STALKER 2: Heart of Chornobyl ’s Cost of Hope expansion arrives with a determinedly furrowed brow; that kind of enthusiastic, if just slightly contrite, look of someone hellbent on righting their own past wrongs.

Of course, most of the open-world shooter’s past crimes are long absolved, if not forgiven immediately on the grounds that they were committed amid an actual war. But Cost of Hope does serve as a second chance for this bleak, beautiful, tense, thrilling, imperfectly brilliant game to address certain omissions it made back in 2024 – even if some of these restorations gleam brighter than others.

It returns us, for instance, to the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant (CNPP), the forbidden ground zero at the heart of STALKER’s mutant-infested, anomaly-ridden vision of Ukraine's Exclusion Zone. Well-trodden ground for the series’ prior instalments, yes, but also such a pivotal locale for this forsaken patch of roasted earth that it was always strange how the base game never ventured near it.

Cost of Hope’s central story also revolves around the rivalry between Zone-hating militiamen Duty and pseudo-anarchists Freedom, another Zone staple that STALKER 2 sidelined in favour of its own younger, sexier factions.

Is this pandering? It doesn’t feel like it. Some returning characters may earn an excited finger-point from Call of Pripyat veterans but they’re typically introduced with a locally appropriate sternness, rather than the smug needle drop of a Marvel post-credits. And Cost of Hope’s added map regions, where you’ll be spending the bulk of its wandering and fighting, are all fine pieces of world design work, regardless of whether you already know what a Myklukha is.

The first of these, the Iron Forest, takes an isolated anomaly from a previous game and expands it into an unsettlingly hostile, sometimes downright ghostly tract of twisted metal and electrical deathtraps. Thick fog seems to choke this place more often than anywhere else in the Zone, while lingering radio signals carry the dead’s last words on the air. It’s awful here, and I love it.

The CNPP doesn’t disappoint either. While the story flow takes you on a grim sightseeing tour through the megalophobia-inducing sarcophagus and the gnarled remains of reactor number four, the whole area is worth exploring. It’s a solemn sprawl of towering industrial tombs - perhaps not as dangerous neighbouring Pripyat, but with longer stretches of silence to truly drink in the tragedy of it.

Best of all is the lost town of Lymansk, which without wanting to spoil too much, is essentially Ravenholm if Remedy Entertainment built it. Trading off the free-roamability of the other new locations for a more focused dive into survival horror, Lymansk has a disregard for the laws of physics that even the main Zone doesn’t muster.

Cost of Hope then asks you to traverse its impossible suburbs in the dark, while striking all your light sources with electronic impotence. It’s unlike anything else in the game, let alone this expansion, and yet creeping through it with dwindling ammo and a broken torch feels like STALKER 2 at its weird, unforgiving best.

Part of that is also down to how the Lymansk section departs from the far, far more common mission loop of hoofing it to some crumbling Soviet facility, blasting all the men/mutants inside, and leaving. Cost of Hope trusts in the process too, and repeatedly.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: The New ‘Wildwood’ Trailer Shows a Mix of Coraline’s Style With a Haunting Fairy Tale
articles.subtitle: Laika’s latest stop motion film has shades of both Coraline and Labyrinth Related Portland, Oregon-based stop-motion animation studio Laika launched in 2009 with Coraline, Henry Selick’s highly acclaimed adaptation of Neil Gaiman’s dark fairy tale about...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Laika’s latest stop motion film has shades of both Coraline and Labyrinth

Related

Portland, Oregon-based stop-motion animation studio Laika launched in 2009 with Coraline, Henry Selick’s highly acclaimed adaptation of Neil Gaiman’s dark fairy tale about a girl who discovers another world where a twisted doppelganger of her mother hopes to keep her forever. The new trailer for the studio’s latest film, Wildwood, shows a return to Laika's roots with an eerie story that combines aspects of Coraline and Jim Henson’s 1986 musical Labyrinth.

Set to a hauntingly slow version of Avicii’s “Wake Me Up,” the trailer introduces Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), the mysterious ruler of an enchanted forest near Portland. Alexandra lost her own son and is so desperate that she sends a murder of crows to abduct an infant from a city playground. Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) journeys into the dangerous woods with her classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay) to rescue her brother Mac, seeking help to face Alexandra and her wolf army.

Labyrinth also followed a young girl journeying to a magical realm to rescue her infant brother after he was abducted by the Goblin King, though in that film she effectively summoned him by wishing goblins would take the crying baby away.

The fairytale setup was also part of Pan’s Labyrinth, where a faun asks a girl to shed her baby brother’s blood to open a portal to another world where she could become a princess. The initial teaser trailer for Wildwood showed Prue’s parents making her promise not to take her brother outside, so it’s possible they know that he came from the woods and are trying to protect him from Alexandra.

Beyond sharing an animation style, Coraline and Wildwood also focus on young women facing tyrannical mother figures. Coraline had assistance from a cat and her young neighbor. While Curtis goes to the woods with Prue, he seems to be having a very bad time. Prue is making allies and riding a giant eagle while Curtis is dressed in the uniform of one of Alexandra’s soldiers and held in a cage.

Wildwood is directed by Travis Knight and written by Chris Butler. The two previously worked together on the 2016 Laika film Kubo and the Two Strings, another family-focused fairy tale following a boy looking for his missing samurai father. The star-studded cast includes Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Angela Bassett, and Charlie Day. Wildwood releases on Oct. 23 through Fathom Entertainment.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: AngryMiao AM Infinity.97 mouse review
articles.subtitle: Flagship speed, boutique flair.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
2026 is shaping up to be an immense year for high-end gaming mice, with everything from the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike to the Razer Viper V4 Pro and the Corsair Sabre V2 Pro proving genuine innovation, with everything from materials to speed and potency all covered off.

So when the AngryMiao AM Infinity.97 came across my desk promising a sub-50 g weight with a 30,000 DPI sensor, 8000 Hz wireless polling and some very innovative battery tech, it definitely piqued my interest.

AngryMiao is a brand I associate more with its keyboards than mice, with it having a penchant for the weird and wacky, opting for sci-fi-type designs in a similar vein to Gravastar. The AM Infinity.97 doesn't deviate from that formula, opting for a very holey chassis with an aggressive look all in the name of both lightness and standing out from a very crowded ultralight mouse market.

It's purposefully been designed to be smaller than other mice to shed weight while keeping things comfortable, shaving three percent off a 'standard' size, hence the 97 in its name—it refers to being 97% of a full mouse.

Buttons: 5 Feet: PTFE Connectivity: 2.4 GHz receiver/Bluetooth, USB-C to USB-A wired Sensor: PixArt PAW3950 Max DPI: 30,000 Max acceleration: 50 g Max speed: 750 IPS Polling rate: 8000 Hz (2.4 GHz) Battery life: Up to 165 hours RGB lighting: 1-zone Warranty: 1 year Price: $189

It's certainly an interesting aesthetic that's helped along in any case by the colour you choose: AngryMiao offers the AM Infinity.97 in black, white or pink. The one I was sent was white, which looks pleasant enough. At first, it seems like there aren't many places where your hand can make contact with the chassis, given the number of holes in the rodent, although you'd be surprised at how comfortable this mouse is when you get it in hand.

AngryMiao states this mouse is designed more for claw grippers than any other type, although I had no issues using a palm or fingertip grip over my couple of weeks with the device. It's a very comfortable rodent to use, and a sub-50 g weight (47 g with the battery) makes this one of the nimblest and lightest mice I've used this year. Take the battery out (more on that later), use it wired, and it can even go down to 39 g.

That lightness doesn't come at the cost of durability, either. The AM Infinity.97 is made of a magnesium-aluminium alloy chassis that feels sturdy to the touch, while the chassis is slightly contoured to fit well in hand and the cool sensation from the metal finish helps with comfort for long-term play sessions.

The button placement here makes sense, with two main options and a scroll wheel on top, and navigation buttons on the side. On the underside is a selector switch between Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz wireless connectivity modes. There isn't a dedicated DPI switch button, which is a bit of a shame, nor is there anything like a DPI clutch on the side. It's functional, but a little minimal.

Nonetheless, I'm a fan of the custom TTC Orange Dot Optical V2 switches the brand has opted for for the AM Infinity.97's main mouse buttons. They've got a very snappy and positive feel under finger, plus have the benefit of being optical, so they're much faster than standard mechanical buttons.

Software duties are handled by a web-based UI and an associated downloadable executable that has the nasty habit of running in the background, potentially sapping away vital system resources. Otherwise, it's lightweight and easy to use, but is quite basic for duties such as setting DPI and polling rate, rebinding buttons, creating macros and profiles, setting parameters such as lift-off distance and acceleration, and that's about it. You get deeper customisation from rivals.

And now to where things matter: performance. AngryMiao has put a 30,000 DPI PixArt PAW3950 sensor inside the AM Infinity.97, which I've tested in other gaming mice over the years, and it provides ample sensitivity and responsiveness to make my usual test runs of Counter-Strike 2 a breeze.

Admittedly, using the full 30,000 DPI on offer all the time is likely to be especially jittery, but you can move it down in software between 100 and the full 30,000 to get a more comfortable level. In my instance, that was between 1600 and 3200 DPI for more accurate aiming in Counter-Strike 2, and for more comfortable navigation in Windows.

Connectivity is handled either by Bluetooth or 2.4 GHz, with the latter supporting the 8000 Hz wireless polling rate. The fact that this mouse also comes with Bluetooth adds some versatility against the competition from the likes of Corsair, which eschews that in favour of outright performance in one device. I found the mouse's connection over either method to be reliable and stable, using Bluetooth on my MacBook Pro and the bundled receiver on my Windows gaming PC.

8000 Hz wireless polling is becoming more of a given at this higher end of the market, rather than just a nice-to-have, and it's present over both wired and 2.4 GHz use. It can be controlled in software for balancing endurance and potency, especially for pro players who are more likely to feel the benefit than us normal folk. It translates to added responsiveness and potentially lower latency, as a higher polling rate means a device reports its position and inputs more frequently (hence Hz as the measurement).

The combination of the lightweight, compact chassis and potent internals makes the AM Infinity.97 easily one of the most responsive gaming mice I've ever tested, alongside Razer's Viper V4 Pro and the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike. It sticks with Razer's idea of doing the basics well, rather than adding haptics and rapid trigger as Logitech does, but makes a fantastic first impression.

Its flagship PixArt sensor feels accurate, while its low mass makes wrist flicks and sweeping movements in CS:2 very easy, plus the optical switches translate to very brisk inputs even without any of the other tech Logitech has packed into its option. This is a rodent that nails the basics to make it a very potent all-rounder.

I realise I've gotten all the way through this copy and have failed to mention the coolest aspect of the AM Infinity.97, which is its swappable batteries. Okay, we've seen this before in headsets and more recently in mice such as the Glorious Model O3 Wireless, but the way AngryMiao does it is a little different.

articles.title: macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 fixed a pretty major screen-sharing flaw
articles.subtitle: Macworld A recent report by the security firm Calif provides details for a security patch that was included in the macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 update released last week. Apple also released macOS 15.7.9 and 14.8.9 updates that provide the same security fix.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
A recent report by the security firm Calif provides details for a security patch that was included in the macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 update released last week. Apple also released macOS 15.7.9 and 14.8.9 updates that provide the same security fix.

While Apple’s release notes state that through the vulnerability, “an attacker on the network may be able to authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials,” Apple doesn’t usually provide details on any found security hole, leaving the explanation to the researchers and others. In this case, the inner workings of the vulnerability were discussed at the Black Hat conference last week.

Screen sharing is a built-in macOS feature that’s quite useful for administering multiple Macs on a network. From one Mac, a user with the proper credentials can log on to another Mac. Screen sharing displays the remote Mac’s desktop as a window on the user’s display.

However, screen sharing had an authentication issue that involved improper state management during authentication. This allowed unauthorized users to try to log on. In its own report, the National Cyber Security in the Netherlands reported that “port 5900 was accessible from the internet.” Port 5900 refers to the TCP port in macOS for screen sharing.

If you are a frequent user of macOS’s screen sharing, it’s important to install the update to patch this vulnerability. Since the update contains only the security fix, it won’t take too long to install, but you will need to restart the Mac.

Macworld has several guides to help, including a guide on whether or not you need antivirus software, a list of Mac viruses, malware, and trojans, and a comparison of Mac security software.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality.

articles.title: "Without us, Bethesda games aren’t Bethesda games": Rallies against Microsoft layoffs at Elder Scrolls studio continue, with unionised devs' morale "on the upswing"
articles.subtitle: "All of a sudden we have yearly layoffs" Yesterday, August 18th, further union rallies against Microsoft's mass layoffs across Xbox studios were held across North America.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
"All of a sudden we have yearly layoffs"

Yesterday, August 18th, further union rallies against Microsoft's mass layoffs across Xbox studios were held across North America. As the One Bethesda Game Studio (OneBGS) union and the Communication Workers of America (CWA)-supported protests continue, one unionised Bethesda developer has said that while work-related morale for those who remain at the studio is low, there's optimism about their efforts to organise.

This latest round of rallies were dubbed Save Our Devs and were held across nine locations in the US and Canada. The likes of Redmond in Washington, Rockville in Maryland, and Austin in Texas have all been the sites of such rallies before, while protests were also held in the likes of Minneapolis and Albany this time.

Around these rallies, two unionised Bethesda developers - lead character artist Alex Nguyen and technical producer Nathan Hahn - have spoken to Kotaku about the current atmosphere at the studio post-cuts. "We actually submitted a proposal to the company on how to perform a reduction in force back in February of this year," Hahn pointed out. "The company sat on that for four months and did not give us a response before performing these layoffs."

Nguyen, meanwhile, refuted suggestions that the layoffs only affected "a whole bunch of middle management", saying that "people on the ground making sure that this game works and putting it in the hands of players" have been let go.

Understandably given the layoffs have further shattered the idea of working at Bethesda and Zenimax being relatively stable and secure, as well as jettisoning veteran staff with valuable institutional knowledge, Hahn said that among remaining staff "morale for our work at our jobs has never been lower". Though, he made clear that morale as it pertains to the devs' efforts to collectively organise is "on the upswing".

The CWA union and their Canadian offshoot CWA Canada filed unfair labour practice complaints against Microsoft over the layoffs via the US National Labour Relations Board (NLRB) last month. The unions accused the company of mishandling the cuts, alleging that Microsoft failed to provide information to the union, engaged in bad faith bargaining, performed "coercive actions", and modified employee contracts.

The layoffs have left the future development timelines of games like The Elder Scrolls 6 and The Elder Scrolls Online looking more nebulous, despite Microsoft's efforts to usher out statements suggesting everything's hunky-dory while revealing a bunch of Elder Scrolls and Fallout games/expansions now in the works.

articles.subtitle: Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate makes one design decision that I would change for MacBooks
articles.subtitle: macOS Golden Gate If there’s one change I could make to iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, it would be disabling the new swipe-down gesture to invoke Siri AI.
articles.author: 9to5Mac
articles.content:
macOS Golden Gate

If there’s one change I could make to iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, it would be disabling the new swipe-down gesture to invoke Siri AI. There are enough ways to summon Siri that don’t break my muscle memory around opening Notification Center on my iPhone and iPad.

Meanwhile, on the Mac, it’s almost all good news with macOS 27 Golden Gate. Even in late August, new betas are still adding delightful changes. Still, there’s one change I’d like to see before macOS 27 is released next month.

MacBook battery percentage is harder to read in macOS 27 Golden Gate

macOS 27 Golden Gate includes a redesigned menu bar control for battery. By default, the percentage isn’t visible. It’s just a battery-shaped visual indicator.

In this state, it looks nice. I run with the percentage off on iPhone, which has the same battery indicator. I’ve always preferred to display the percentage on Mac, though.

If you flip the ‘show percentage’ toggle on in macOS 27 Golden Gate, it puts the number inside the battery. I believe this is to be consistent with what the iPhone does in iOS 27.

Putting the percentage inside the battery icon on iPhone is Apple’s density solution for cornering everything to the right of the notch or Dynamic Island. On the Mac, this screen real estate issue isn’t present for me — even in the menu bar.

I’ve been running macOS 27 Golden Gate on my 15-inch MacBook Air since day one of the first developer beta. What I’ve found is that I’m generally less aware of my battery percentage because it’s less legible for my eyes.

I hope Apple revisits this design decision in the future, especially if it’s an issue for more users. In the meantime, I’ve at least resolved the issue for myself.

Using Codex, I made a simple menu bar utility that reliably presents the current battery state and percentage with the visual clarity that I expect. If that’s something that may be helpful for you as well, you can download and install it for free here.

It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence

A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Subnautica 2's latest 1.2 update is friend focused—finally adding the key mechanic to any great multiplayer game
articles.subtitle: Nothing's impossible when you have the power of friendship.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
I'm not sure there's been a better invention for multiplayer games than proximity chat. Whether it be friends screaming vengeance down the side of a mountain after you abandon them in Peak, or the wails of one of your fellow workers fall suspiciously silent in Lethal Company. Proximity chat offers up fertile ground for hilariously wacky and memorable multiplayer moments, so you can imagine my excitement when I found out it's coming to Subnautica 2.

"This is going to let you have an in-game voice chat option that you can do with your friends," Anthony Gallegos, creative director, says in a dev diary. "You'll be able to talk locally with each other and then as you get further away you'll hear a switch to sort of a radio-sounding voice, and you'll progressively break up as you get further away, up until a certain point where you can almost not hear me at all."

Now, you can use your friends as a canary, sending them down into dark caves and listening to see if anything's amiss. At the very least, Gallegos believes it will "definitely add to the tension of" exploring the formidable alien ocean.

But that's not all being added to Subnautica 2 in its next update. The whole patch seems friend-focused. There's player emotes that will "let you roll through a bunch of different emotions, so you can cheer on your friends, clap at them to tell them that you're happy with them, or maybe that you're a little annoyed with them, and you can also show that you're frustrated.

"The thing that I think is the most exciting about these is actually the ways that people will use them out of context that I think will make for some really fun moments."

Players can also look forward to better inventory sharing, which means you won't have to go searching for discarded loot that your friends leave behind. Instead, all you have to do now is go up behind your pal and access their stash from their backpack—quick and efficient. Although, thieves-be-warned, "the person whose inventory is being accessed will get a little notification" so pickpocketing is out of the question, unless you have an especially unobservant friend.

The last major feature coming with 1.2 will be player revives. Now, if you're playing with a group and get lost, or get too hungry and pass out, your friends will have a short amount of time to swim over to you, share their oxygen, and revive you back to the world of the living. It's such a helpful feature that I'm honestly pretty surprised Subnautica 2 didn't have it before.

All in all, update 1.2 seems like a helpful pitstop on the way to more significant changes, which feels But it is a pitstop that was very necessary before the map gets any bigger and more challenging to navigate: "Alongside all of this we're continuing work on the Early Access 2 update that's going to add the new region with the new story, and the new progression, and the new vehicles, all those things."

The US Capitol is currently dealing with a new kind of problem as more lawmakers turn to chatbots to write their proposed laws. According to a recent report, the US House Office of Legislative Counsel is getting flooded with AI-generated bills that are packed with careless errors. Instead of speeding things up, this new habit is actually forcing lawyers to spend extra hours fixing bad drafts.

Lawyers spend extra hours fixing basic mistakes in new bills

More and more congressional offices are using general chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude to write their legislative proposals. While this sounds like a great shortcut, the people who actually have to review these documents are not happy. Lawyers at the Office of Legislative Counsel now say they are spending way more time cleaning up machine-made drafts than they would if they just wrote the bills from scratch.

The problem comes down to the tiny details that matter in lawmaking. These artificial intelligence tools often miss crucial nuances. For example, a chatbot might not understand the difference between a tax credit, a tax deduction, or a simple grant. It might also use the word “state” in a way that accidentally leaves out Washington DC and tribal nations. On top of that, lawyers are catching fictional or incorrect references to older laws buried in the text.

articles.title: Review: SuperDuper! 4 gets a stem-to-stern revamp, but is just as seaworthy as ever
articles.subtitle: Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper!…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper! to ensure that all my data is safe and sound. And now, for the first time in a very long time, the venerable backup utility has gotten a top-to-bottom update that brings it into the modern era without sacrificing any of the features—and, most importantly, the reliability—that its users have come to depend on.

While SuperDuper! 4 may look like an entirely new beast, its history has stuck around. It still explains what it’s doing in plain English. It still allows you to make complete, bootable backups. It still has its excellent Smart Update option to optimize the copying process.

But it’s gotten some significant updates too. There’s a new interface, for starters, which conforms to Apple’s current Liquid Glass aesthetic, love it or hate it. It’s a bit of a shock to the system after so long without a change, but it’s hard to deny that the old look had grown somewhat antiquated. The result is an app that makes backups as simple and straightforward as they should be, so that anyone can figure it out: click here to set your destination, choose what method, and click Go.

The changes to SuperDuper! 4 also run more than just skin deep. For example, it’s considerably faster than the previous version—up to an order magnitude faster using the new Turbo implementation of Smart Update, according to Shirt Pocket. That’s borne out in my real-world usage. For example, my last nightly backup of 20.55GB took less than 4 minutes.

There are new capabilities here, too. A new Preview feature lets you perform a dry run of your copy job, letting you see every file that will be changed without actually doing any of it. With a new background helper app, copies won’t interrupt whatever you’re doing. And there’s Shortcuts support, so you can run a workflow when your copy job is completed—or even have one of your shortcuts kick off a copy job.

I’ve been using betas of SuperDuper! 4 for a month or so now, and what’s impressed me most is how much it maintains that set-it-and-forget-it strength of the previous versions. The most important thing for a backup is that element of reliability, so when I open up the app and see “31 successful in a row” note, I know that my data is right where it should be.

And if something goes wrong, it’s easier than ever to see what happened: click on a failed job and you’ll get the details, including an Apple Intelligence-powered summary of the job. (You can get that for completed jobs too. )

There are way more features here too, ones that I just don’t have much reason to use for my purposes, but might just well be what you’re looking for. For example, copy rules that let you handle certain files and folders in granular ways, such as excluding certain ones from backups; support for any file system that macOS understands; and there’s support for multiple copy jobs at the same time, even for those that are scheduled.

Backup apps may not be the most exciting software category, but I dare you to find one that’s more crucial. For me, SuperDuper! has done the job for years and I’ve never had any reason to complain about it. Nothing about that seems poised to change with version 4.

SuperDuper! 4 requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later. A free trial version lets you make unlimited full erase backups, but to unlock the rest of the features requires a one-time payment of $43.95. There’s also an upgrade discount for owners of SuperDuper 3 of up to 30 percent. (And, if you bought version 3 very recently, you may be able to get version 4 for free.) And good news: if you need to run backups on older systems, SuperDuper 3 is sticking around.

For everybody who’s already backing up their Macs, SuperDuper! 4 may offer some new features and speed increases that will make the process even smoother. For those of you who aren’t yet…what are you waiting for?
